opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and it's one where our everyday language kind of trips us up. Most of what people call "taste" is actually smell. Your tongue really only detects a handful of things: sweet, salty, sour, bitter, umami, maybe a few others depending on who you ask. But the richness of flavor, what makes a strawberry taste like a strawberry rather than just "sweet and a little sour," that's almost entirely coming from your nose.

There are actually two routes for smell. There's orthonasal olfaction, which is sniffing: molecules come in through your nostrils from the outside world. And then there's retronasal olfaction, where, when you're chewing and swallowing, volatile molecules travel up the back of your throat into your nasal cavity. Your brain stitches that together with what's happening on your tongue, along with texture and temperature, and it presents the whole thing to you as if it's happening in your mouth. So flavor is really this multisensory construct, and smell is the dominant ingredient. The classic demonstration is to pinch your nose and eat a jellybean. You'll get sweet, but you often can't tell what flavor it is until you let go.

Fragrance, then, is in a sense the same underlying sense applied to a different context. It's the same receptors, the same olfactory system, and often even overlapping molecules. A lot of the same compounds show up in perfumes and in food flavorings. Vanillin is vanillin whether it's in ice cream or in a fragrance. The difference is mostly about intent and delivery: whether you're designing something to be experienced through the nose from the outside, on skin or in a room, or through the mouth while eating.

From where I sit, all of these share the same core scientific problem: you have a molecule, or more realistically a mixture of hundreds of molecules, and you want to predict what a human will perceive. With vision we've mapped that for a long time; we know how wavelengths relate to color. With smell, we've historically had no such map. That's a big part of what motivated our work: building models that go from molecular structure to perceived odor, a kind of principal odor map. If you can do that well, it's useful whether you're working on flavors, fragrances, or even things like insect repellents, because underneath it's the same sense and the same physics and chemistry.

r001.rationale: The response says flavor’s richness comes mostly from smell and explains that with the nose pinched, a person can detect sweetness but often cannot identify the flavor.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, because the terminology trips people up constantly. Let me try to untangle it.

Smell is the sense. It's the biology. It's the fact that you have around four hundred different types of receptors in your nose, each one encoded by a different gene, and when volatile molecules come in and bind to those receptors, your brain turns that pattern of activation into a perception. That's olfaction. It's one of the oldest senses we have, and honestly it's the one we understand the least.

Flavor is what happens when you eat. And here's the thing most people don't realize: the vast majority of what you call "taste" is actually smell. Your tongue can only really do five things, maybe six if you count fat. Sweet, salty, sour, bitter, umami. That's it. Everything else, the difference between a strawberry and a raspberry, the difference between a Cabernet and a Pinot, that's all coming from aroma molecules traveling up the back of your throat into your nasal cavity. We call that retronasal olfaction. So flavor is really the integration of taste, smell, and some trigeminal stuff like the heat of chili or the cooling of mint, but smell is doing most of the heavy lifting. If you've ever had a bad cold and food tastes like cardboard, you've run that experiment on yourself.

Fragrance, then, is smell as a designed artifact. It's the industry side. It's perfumery, it's the scent in your laundry detergent, your shampoo, the air in a hotel lobby. People think of it as perfume bottles, but it's enormous. Basically every consumer product you touch has been deliberately scented by someone, and there's a whole profession, perfumers, who are essentially composers working in this invisible medium.

So the way I'd frame the relationship is: smell is the underlying sensory channel, and flavor and fragrance are two application domains built on top of it. One is what goes in your mouth, one is what goes on your body or in your environment. And what's wild is that the industry actually splits along those lines. The big companies all have a flavor division and a fragrance division, and they often operate almost like separate companies, even though at the chemical level they're working with overlapping palettes of the same molecules. A lot of the same compounds show up on both sides. Vanillin is in your dessert and in your perfume.

From a machine learning perspective, what got me excited is that this is a case where the underlying problem is unified even if the human organizations aren't. If you can build a model that goes from molecular structure to how something smells, that model doesn't care whether it's being used to design a beverage or a candle. It's the same map from chemistry to perception. And for a long time we just didn't have that map at all. We had it for color, we had it for sound, you could tell me a wavelength and I could tell you what you'd see. For smell, nobody could look at a molecule and tell you what it smelled like. That's the gap we've been trying to close.

r001.rationale: The response says that during a bad cold, when smell is impaired, food tastes like cardboard, clearly conveying that flavor experience is severely impaired.

astra-6.text:
I think of smell as the common thread connecting flavor and fragrance. Flavor is a combination of what your tongue detects—sweet, sour, salty, bitter, umami—and what your nose detects, along with things like texture and temperature. When you chew, volatile molecules travel from your mouth up into your nose. That’s called retronasal olfaction, and it’s a huge part of what we experience as flavor. It’s why food seems so much less flavorful when your nose is congested.

Fragrance involves that same sense of smell, but typically you’re encountering the molecules by breathing them in through your nostrils. So these feel like different experiences—eating something versus smelling a perfume—but they share a sensory foundation. The context and the other senses involved help determine how we experience them.

r001.rationale: The response says food seems “so much less flavorful” when the nose is congested, conveying severe flavor impairment when smell is impaired.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of smell as the underlying sense, and flavor and fragrance as two different ways we experience it. Flavor is what happens when smell combines with taste and the other sensations you get in your mouth—texture, temperature, the heat of a chili pepper. Taste gives you things like sweet, sour, salty, bitter, and umami. But much of what makes a strawberry taste like a strawberry is actually smell.

When you chew, volatile molecules travel from your mouth up into your nose. That’s called retronasal olfaction, and your brain integrates it with taste so seamlessly that you experience it as coming from your mouth. Fragrance typically involves smelling through your nostrils, from the outside world. So there’s a shared sensory system underneath both, but the route those molecules take and the context in which you experience them can be quite different.

r001.rationale: The response says smell contributes much of flavor, but it does not state that flavor is severely impaired when a person cannot smell.
